confidence_note: December 1943 Santa Fe vacation, the daughter's question and the 1948 camera are consistent across Berger's blog piece and other accounts. The one-hour walk, the 'darkroom inside the camera' what-if (Berger's own framing, not a Land quote) and the 1943-to-1973 line come from Berger's strategy+business article, not the book text. Daughter's name Jennifer is from RNZ, not Berger, so not used. Old scripted dialogue and the 'better film vs instant photo' pair were dropped.
facts: 1943, family vacation (another account says summer; Berger article says December, so year only) in Santa Fe: Edwin Land took a photo of his daughter, who was three, and she asked why she could not see it right away.
An expert would have answered that this is how the camera works; Land took the question seriously instead.
Land went for a walk and within an hour had the what-if of instant photography; Berger frames it as: what if you could have a darkroom inside a camera?
The practical details took much longer; in Land's words the work ran from 1943 to 1973.
The first Polaroid camera went on sale on 26 November 1948, five years after the question.
Berger sets Why, What if, How as a logical progression; the daughter's question is the why, the walk the what-if, the years after the how.
Closed questions (how many, how much, how fast) keep the status quo; Berger says why is the one companies ask least.
Polaroid filed for bankruptcy in 2001, a casualty of the digital shift; Berger presents it as a warning about relying on closed questions.
Berger says schools and business cultures tend to reward rote answers over questions.
Land later said he set about solving the puzzle his daughter had set him (RNZ).

Berger traces other breakthroughs to a question: in the Gatorade story a college football coach asked why players weren't urinating more, which led to realizing sweating players weren't replenishing fluids well enough.

Land's company became one of the Nifty Fifty growth stocks of the 1960s; Berger traces Netflix and Pixar to founding questions; Hal Gregersen (cited) found innovative leaders like Jobs and Bezos question everything.
scene_details: a family vacation in Santa Fe in 1943
a walk of about an hour
tension: A stock answer was available for a three-year-old's question; Land took it as a real problem.
opening_idea: A three-year-old wants to see a photo now and the correct answer fits in a sentence.

lessons.idea: Keep a question beside the work before giving the stock answer; the question often yields a list of things that could change.
lessons.anchor: Land's daughter asked why; he did not stop at 'that's how the camera works'.

reflect_final: If you asked why about one thing at work that everyone explains with 'that's how we do it', what would you hope to find out?

use_cases.situation: The team defends a process with 'we have always done it this way'
use_cases.move: Mention Land's daughter and propose a few minutes asking why this step exists.

use_cases.situation: Your child asks why and you have a stock answer
use_cases.move: Admit you never asked it and wonder together what if it were different.

use_cases.situation: You notice you are doing a familiar task on autopilot
use_cases.move: Ask why in this order and add one what-if.

pocket_idea: Land answered his daughter's why with a walk, not a stock answer.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A three-year-old's 'why can't I see it now' led to the Polaroid camera five years later.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Santa Fe 1943, the daughter's question, the walk, 1948.
